lines: LIKE A BULLET LEAVING A GUN.
IT DOESN'T EVEN HAVE TO HIT YOU.
THE FISH WITH A TRANSPARENT HEAD

segments.text: This shrimp punches like a bullet leaving a gun — and it doesn't even have to hit you to hurt you.
Meet the peacock mantis shrimp. Four inches long, and its front claws don't swing — they're cocked like a loaded spring, then released.
That release hits with about 1,500 newtons of force — accelerating faster than a bullet leaving a rifle barrel.
Around ten thousand times the pull of gravity — fast enough to reach roughly fifty miles an hour, underwater.

segments.text: The claw moves so fast it boils a pocket of water behind it. When that bubble collapses, it delivers a second, invisible punch — even if the claw itself misses.
For a fraction of a millisecond, that collapse reaches temperatures in the same range as the surface of the sun — in a flash of light called sonoluminescence.
Scientists only measured this directly for the first time in February 2025 — a laser experiment at Northwestern confirmed what researchers had predicted a decade earlier.
